    01       REPRODUCTIVE RIGHTS


Termination of Minor's Pregnancy
SC vs AIIMS — Foeticide Argument vs Bodily Autonomy

Court: Supreme Court of India | Law: MTP Act, 1971

 – SC refused AIIMS curative petition to stop 15-yr-old rape survivor's 30-week abortion.
 – Centre's stand: Termination beyond 24 weeks is 'akin to foeticide'; push for carrying to full term + adoption.
 – ASG Aishwarya Bhati (for AIIMS): Pressed for 'four more weeks' in interest of minor and foetus.
 – Jan 2024 — Delhi HC recalled order allowing 32-week pregnant widow to abort.
 – Jul 2025 — 16-yr-old rape survivor: HC 'suggested' carrying to full term; minor agreed.
 – Oct 2023 — SC split on 27-yr-old's case; Justice Hima Kohli asked 'stop foetal heartbeat'; 3-judge bench
   rescinded abortion order.
 – Apr 2024 — SC allowed 14-yr-old survivor to abort at 31 weeks: risk of continuing > risk of termination.
 – MTP Act: Termination allowed up to 24 weeks. Beyond 24 Medical Board in 'approved facility' required.
 – Medical Board process cumbersome women approach courts directly.

Key Laws MTP Act 1971 · Section 3 (24-week limit) · Medical Board requirement post-24 weeks
CLAT Angle Reproductive rights · Article 21 (bodily autonomy) · MTP Act limits · SC discretion in medical matters


   02        INSOLVENCY LAW


Vedanta vs Adani — Jaypee NCLAT Ruling
Commercial Wisdom of CoC Prevails Over Highest NPV Bid

Court: NCLAT | Law: IBC, 2016

 – JAL entered insolvency June 2024 — defaulted on Rs 57,000 crore loans.
 – CIRP: Resolution Professional takes control; CoC (Committee of Creditors) governs under IBC.
 – Sept 2025: Vedanta had highest NPV (~Rs 12,505 crore) after Challenge Process bidding.
 – Nov 2025: Adani's plan got overwhelming CoC majority despite Vedanta's higher NPV.
 – Vedanta sent last-minute addendum after voting began — CoC rejected as process violation.
 – NCLAT: Addendum = modification, not clarification. Process Note 'clearly prohibited' late changes.
 – Adani won because: better upfront cash, timing, and execution feasibility scores.
 – Key principle: CoC not bound to select highest bid — 'commercial wisdom' of lenders is final.
 – Judicial review limited to IBC Sec 30(2) & 61(3) — 'material irregularity' standard only.

Key Laws IBC 2016 · Sections 30(2), 61(3) · CoC 'commercial wisdom' doctrine
CLAT Angle IBC process · CoC powers · judicial restraint in commercial matters · CIRP timeline


   03        MARITIME LAW


Bombay HC Frees 50 Sailors — Shadow Fleet Ships
Habeas Corpus in a High-Seas Humanitarian Crisis

Court: Bombay High Court | Law: Customs Act · Merchant Shipping Act · BNS 2023

 – 3 vessels — MT Asphalt Star, MT Stellar Ruby, MT Al Jafzia — detained since February.
 – Shadow fleet: vessels using deceptive practices to move sanctioned goods (Iran, Russia, Venezuela oil).
 – Evasion tactics: Switch off AIS transponders, 'spoof' GPS, change names/flags/company.
 – ~3,000 such vessels globally; often 15–20 yrs old, barely seaworthy, substandard insurance.
 – MT Asphalt Star: Illegally transferred 30 MT fuel oil + 5,473 MT bitumen inside India's EEZ.



                                                     CLAT 2027 Preparation · @CLAT_Vision

@CLAT_Vision                                               Law Articles · May 2026                                  Page 3


 – 50 Indian crew survived on 300 ml water/day, burned wood to cook — abandoned since Feb 9.
 – Crew filed habeas corpus Apr 23: 'floating wrongful confinement in subhuman conditions.'
 – HC (Justices Ghuge & Venegavkar): Seafarers cannot be detained against their will.

Key Laws Habeas Corpus · AIS (Automatic Identification System) · EEZ (200 nautical miles) · Merchant Shipping Act
CLAT Angle Habeas corpus · maritime law · EEZ concept · humanitarian rights of detained seafarers


   04         DISABILITY RIGHTS


SC Expands 'Acid Attack Victim' Definition
Forced Acid Ingestion Now Covered Under RPwD Act 2016

Court: Supreme Court of India | Law: RPwD Act, 2016

 – SC: Survivors forced to consume acid (internal injuries, no external scarring) = acid attack victims under RPwD
   Act.
 – Bench: CJI Surya Kant + Justice Joymalya Bagchi. Applies retrospectively.
 – Old definition [Schedule 2(zc)]: 'Disfigured due to violent assaults by throwing of acid' — excluded ingestion
   victims.
 – No disability certificate = no financial aid, rehabilitation, or medical support.
 – Petition (Shaheen Malik): Article 14 violation — same harm, different method, arbitrary exclusion.
 – BNS 2024 Sec 124: Throwing and administering acid = same offence. RPwD distinction was incoherent.
 – SC directed: Reverse burden of proof on accused; acid sellers to be made co-accused.
 – Trial backlog: UP tops with 198 pending cases; West Bengal 160; Gujarat 114.

Key Laws RPwD Act 2016 · Schedule 2(zc) · BNS 2024 Sec 124 · Articles 14 & 21
CLAT Angle Disability law · purposive interpretation · Article 14 classification · Article 21 dignity


   05         CONSUMER LAW


Medical Negligence Claims Don't Die with the Doctor
Pecuniary Claims Survive Death — actio personalis Maxim Clarified

Court: Supreme Court of India | Law: Consumer Protection Act 1986 · Succession Act 1925

 – SC: Medical negligence case does NOT end automatically on accused doctor's death.
 – Bench: Justices JK Maheshwari + Atul Chandurkar. Original case: 1990 eye surgery, Bihar.
 – Personal claims (pain, suffering) abate on death. Pecuniary/financial claims survive against estate.
 – Common law maxim: 'actio personalis moritur cum persona' — personal right dies with the person.
 – Succession Act 1925 Sec 306: Rights to sue survive except defamation, assault, personal injuries not causing
   death.
 – NCDRC 2001 Balbir Singh Makol ruling overruled — had wrongly barred all medical negligence claims
   post-death.
 – SC: 'Scope of exception cannot chew the enabling provision.'
 – Matter remanded to NCDRC to determine negligence and recoverable claims.

Key Laws Consumer Protection Act 1986 · Succession Act 1925 Sec 306 · Order XXII CPC · actio personalis
CLAT Angle Consumer law · survivability of claims · legal maxims · pecuniary vs personal rights

   06        CRIMINAL LAW


Bombay HC Upholds Acquittal in Sohrabuddin Encounter Case
22 Accused Acquitted — CBI Evidence Insufficient, Witnesses Hostile

Court: Bombay High Court | Law: CrPC Sec 197 · Evidence Act · CBI Act

 – Sohrabuddin Sheikh, wife Kausar Bi, associate Tulsiram Prajapati — fake encounter, Nov 2005, Ahmedabad.
 – Special CBI Court Dec 2018: All 22 acquitted including 21 police from Gujarat, Rajasthan, AP.
 – CBI failed to produce 'documentary and substantive evidence'; no sanction obtained under CrPC Sec 197.
 – 92 of 200+ witnesses turned hostile. Judge: CBI 'did what was required to reach a premeditated goal.'
 – Sohrabuddin's brothers' appeals (Apr 2019) rejected by HC after 7 years (concluded Jan 2026).
 – HC (CJ Shree Chandrashekhar bench): No merit in appeals. Acquittals stand.
 – Notable earlier discharges: Amit Shah (2014); IPS officers Dinesh MN, Rajkumar Pandiyan, DG Vanzara.

Key Laws CrPC Sec 197 (sanction for prosecution) · Evidence Act — hostile witnesses · CBI Act
CLAT Angle Criminal procedure · prosecution sanction · evidence standards · encounter jurisprudence


    07       CONSTITUTIONAL LAW


Governor's Role in Swearing-In Delay — Tamil Nadu
TVK Vijay vs Governor Arlekar: Article 164 Under Scrutiny

Court: TN Political Crisis 2026 · Past SC Rulings | Law: Constitution Article 164

 – TN Governor Arlekar delayed swearing-in of TVK leader Vijay as CM despite winning election.
 – Governor demanded 118-MLA proof; TVK has only 108 + Congress 5 = 113 (short of majority mark).
 – Article 164: CM appointed by Governor; ministers on CM's advice; hold office during Governor's pleasure.
 – Constitutional convention: Largest party invited floor test as ultimate check.
 – 2018 Karnataka: SC refused stay on Yediyurappa swearing-in; advanced floor test to 36 hours.
 – 2016 Uttarakhand: SC called floor test the 'ultimate' option in the Harish Rawat case.
 – Former Law Minister Ashwani Kumar: Move is 'a graceless stratagem' and 'a constitutional heresy.'

Key Laws Article 164 (CM appointment) · Article 174 · 10th Schedule · Floor test doctrine
CLAT Angle Governor's discretion · constitutional conventions · Article 164 · floor test jurisprudence


   08        ELECTION LAW


'Tyranny of the Elected' — SC on EC Appointment Law
Election Commissioners (Appointment) Act 2023 Under Challenge

Court: Supreme Court of India | Law: Article 324(2) · EC Appointment Act 2023

 – SC (May 7): Decades-long delay in enacting EC appointment law described as 'tyranny of the elected.'
 – Bench: Justices Dipankar Datta + Satish Chandra Sharma.
 – 2023 Act: CJI replaced by Union Cabinet minister on selection panel executive holds 2 of 3 seats.
 – Anoop Baranwal v UoI (2023 SC): Interim panel = PM + Leader of Opposition + CJI.
 – EC is 'guardian of democracy' — must be insulated from executive control.
 – Sec 8(2) of 2023 Act: Selection committee can pick 'any other person' — unchecked discretion.
 – Right to vote = part of free speech under Article 19(1)(a) (per Anoop Baranwal ruling).

Key Laws Article 324(2) · EC Appointment Act 2023 · Anoop Baranwal v UoI (2023) · Art 19(1)(a)
CLAT Angle EC independence · Article 324 · separation of powers · appointment reforms

   09        PROPERTY LAW


SC Orders DDA to Refund Rs 165 Crore for Land It Didn't Own
What Happens When Government Sells Lapsed Acquisition?

Court: Supreme Court of India | Law: Land Acquisition Act 2013 · Order XIII-A CPC

 – 2007: Company paid Rs 165 crore for DDA plot at public auction. Paid taxes for a decade.
 – 2015: Original owner Simla Devi filed writ — DDA acquisition had lapsed (she never got compensation).
 – SC 2017 upheld lapse under LA Act 2013 Sec 24(2): 5 years elapsed, compensation unpaid title reverts.
 – DDA then asked buyer to pay again for fresh acquisition — effectively charging twice for same land.
 – SC Apr 29: Ordered refund of Rs 164.91 crore + 7.5% interest from July 2007.
 – DDA argued 'return possession first, then refund' — SC: 'defence is fanciful and illusory.'
 – Order XIII-A CPC: Summary judgment when no real prospect of success; full trial not needed.
 – Restitution principle: When basis of transaction collapses, parties restored to original positions.

Key Laws LA Act 2013 Sec 24(2) · Order XIII-A CPC (summary judgment) · Restitution doctrine
CLAT Angle Property law · land acquisition lapse · restitution · good-faith buyer rights · summary judgment


    10       PERSONAL LAW


How Mizo Marriage Law Keeps Women Out
2026 Amendment Strips Protection from Women Marrying Outside Tribe

Court: Supreme Court (Petition pending) | Law: Mizo Marriage, Divorce & Inheritance Act 2014 (amended 2026)

 – Original 2014 Act: Applied to any Mizo tribe member AND marriages where male member is Mizo.
 – 2026 Amendment: Act applies ONLY if both parties are Mizo OR the male is Mizo.
 – Impact: Mizo woman marrying non-Mizo man loses all protection. Mizo man marrying non-Mizo = still
   protected.
 – Mizo identity (Sec 3m) now traced only through paternal lineage — mother's Mizo identity irrelevant.
 – Sec 25 (sumchhuah divorce): Woman's property share now capped at 50% max; earlier uncapped.
 – Sec 26 (mak divorce): Protection 'personal property of woman shall not be disturbed' — deleted.
 – Petition: Violates Articles 14 (equal protection), 15 (sex discrimination), 21 (dignity).

Key Laws Articles 14, 15, 21 · Mizo Marriage Act 2014 (amended 2026) · Tribal personal law
CLAT Angle Personal law · gender discrimination · tribal identity · property rights · Articles 14-15-21


      11     ELECTION LAW


Madras HC Barred TVK MLA from Floor Test
One Vote · EVM Discrepancy · Article 329(b) Narrow Exception

Court: Madras High Court · SC (listed urgently) | Law: Article 329(b) · RoP Act 1951

 – TVK MLA Sethupathi won No.185 Tiruppattur by exactly ONE vote over DMK's Periakaruppan.
 – Discrepancy: 18 EVM votes difference in two official records; one postal ballot misrouted.
 – EC admitted: No statutory mechanism to transfer a wrongly sent postal ballot between constituencies.
 – HC restrained Sethupathi from participating in any floor test or confidence motion 'until further orders.'
 – Article 329(b): Courts cannot entertain election disputes except through election petition under RoP Act.
 – HC narrow exception (EC v Ashok Kumar 2000): Intervention allowed to preserve evidence or remove obstacles.
 – HC: 'Democracy breathes through the ballot. Courts must walk with constitutional caution.'


                                                      CLAT 2027 Preparation · @CLAT_Vision

@CLAT_Vision                                                Law Articles · May 2026                               Page 6


 – Key reasoning: If his vote proves decisive and election is later invalidated, consequences cannot be undone.

Key Laws Article 329(b) · RoP Act 1951 Secs 80 & 100 · Rule 54A(2) · EC v Ashok Kumar (2000 SC)
CLAT Angle Election disputes · Art 329 bar on courts · electoral integrity · preservation of electoral material


     12      LINGUISTIC RIGHTS


SC Endorses Right to Be Taught in Mother Tongue
Rajasthani Language Case — Articles 350A, 21A, 19(1)(a) Applied

Court: Supreme Court of India | Law: Articles 350A, 21A, 19(1)(a) · RTE Act 2009

 – SC May 12: Children cannot be denied education in language they understand — 'matter of existential rights.'
 – Bench: Justices Vikram Nath + Sandeep Mehta. Directed Rajasthan to frame Rajasthani language policy.
 – Rajasthani spoken by tens of millions — NOT in 8th Schedule of Constitution.
 – Rajasthan's defence: Only 8th Schedule languages taught in govt schools. SC: 'lackadaisical response.'
 – Article 350A: State must provide mother-tongue instruction at primary stage for linguistic minorities.
 – RTE Act Sec 29(2)(f): Teaching in alien tongue 'risks impairing foundational development.'
 – Article 19(1)(a): Language is 'the very essence of an individual.'
 – Article 14: Rajasthan includes Gujarati, Punjabi, Sindhi in curriculum but excludes Rajasthani — arbitrary.

Key Laws Articles 350A, 21A, 19(1)(a), 14 · RTE Act Sec 29(2)(f) · NEP 2020
CLAT Angle Linguistic rights · 8th Schedule · RTE · mother tongue education · Article 350A significance


     13      DIGITAL LAW


Who Owns a Person's Digital Data After Death?
Gandhinagar Court: iCloud Data = Inheritable Property

Court: Civil Court, Gandhinagar | Law: Succession Act 1925 · DPDP Act 2023 · IT Act 2000

 – Family couldn't access deceased man's locked iPhone + iCloud (photos, videos, documents, contacts).
 – Apple: Will assist only with court order appointing a legal representative.
 – Judge Himanshu Choudhary: Appointed daughter as administrator; directed Apple to assist.
 – Held: 'Digital data in iCloud constitutes a valuable digital asset forming part of the estate.'
 – Legal basis: General Clauses Act — movable property = 'every description except immovable.'
 – IT Act Sec 2(47A): Cryptocurrencies and NFTs already recognised as virtual digital assets.
 – DPDP Act 2023 Sec 14: Without nominee, data rights devolve on legal heirs after death.
 – Privacy limit: Right to privacy is 'inherently personal — extinguishes with the individual.'

Key Laws Succession Act 1925 · DPDP Act 2023 Sec 14 · IT Act Sec 2(47A) · General Clauses Act
CLAT Angle Digital property · succession law · privacy after death · DPDP Act · intangible property


    14       CONSTITUTIONAL LAW


SC Cites 'Hinduism as Way of Life' — Revisiting the 1995 Ruling
Sabarimala Hearing Revives Hindutva Election Case Debate

Court: SC — 9-Judge Constitution Bench | Law: RoP Act 1951 Secs 123(3) & 123(3A)

 – During Sabarimala hearing, Justice BV Nagarathna cited 1995: 'Hinduism is a way of life.'
 – 1995 case origin: 1987 Vile Parle by-election; Shiv Sena chief Bal Thackeray's three communal speeches.
 – Speeches: 'Election for protection of Hinduism'; derogatory Muslim references; Hindu unity appeals.
 – Bombay HC: Speeches = corrupt practices under RoP Act Secs 123(3) & 123(3A).


                                                      CLAT 2027 Preparation · @CLAT_Vision

@CLAT_Vision                                              Law Articles · May 2026                                 Page 7


 – SC upheld: Election law cannot be defeated by 'indirect phrasing or coded language.'
 – SC on Hindutva: 'Diverse conglomerate of doctrines and way of life' — using the word ≠ automatic Sec 123
   violation.
 – Full original phrase (rarely cited): 'Hinduism is a way of life, and nothing more' — context was secularism.
 – BJP later cited judgment as endorsement of Hindutva = secularism — controversy continues.

Key Laws RoP Act 1951 · Secs 123(3) & 123(3A) · Article 19(2) · Hindutva case 1995
CLAT Angle Election law · corrupt practices · religious appeals · Hindutva case · secularism doctrine


    15       ENVIRONMENTAL LAW


Forest Rights & Great Nicobar Mega-Project
Calcutta HC Hears PIL on FRA Violations — Shompen Tribe Rights

Court: Calcutta HC (Port Blair bench) | Law: FRA 2006 · PESA Act · Environment Protection Act

 – Rs 81,000 crore GNI project: township, transshipment port, power plant, dual-use airport.
 – PIL May 8: Former IAS officer Meena Gupta alleges systematic FRA 2006 violations.
 – SDLC constituted illegally — only 1 Nicobarese member; FRA requires min 2/3 ST members incl 1 woman.
 – Gram Sabha 'consent': Passed by settler panchayats, NOT tribal Gram Sabhas as required by FRA.
 – RoFR certificate issued Aug 2022 ('all rights settled') — challenged as fraudulent.
 – Forest diversion: 166.10 sq km — 121.87 sq km protected forest, 8.88 sq km deemed forest.
 – Shompen tribe (uncontacted, semi-nomadic): Three settlements in proposed development zone.
 – Shompen 'consent': Obtained through govt officer (AAJVS), not from Shompen. Revoked Nov 2022.

Key Laws FRA 2006 · PESA Sec 5 (Gram Sabha consent) · PVTG rights · Environment Protection Act
CLAT Angle Forest rights · tribal consent · environmental clearance · FRA 2006 · PVTG protection


    16       FAMILY LAW


Rajasthan HC: 'Atta Satta' = Mutual Hostage-Taking
'Familial Extortion Disguised as Custom' — Child Marriage & Forced Consent

Court: Rajasthan High Court (Division Bench) | Law: Hindu Marriage Act 1955 · PoCA 2006 · DV Act 2005

 – Atta satta: Families 'exchange' daughters — two weddings linked, one fate tied to the other.
 – Case: Kiran Bishnoi married Sunil Kumar; simultaneously Sunil's minor sister Suman married Kiran's brother.
 – Suman on attaining majority refused matrimonial home triggered harassment and dowry demands on Kiran.
 – Family court dismissed Kiran's divorce — said she 'voluntarily deserted' and used litigation as leverage.
 – HC: Lower court wrongly treated Suman's decision as justification for harassing Kiran.
 – Standard of proof for matrimonial cruelty: 'Preponderance of probabilities' — NOT beyond reasonable doubt.
 – HC: 'Continued residence under compulsion ≠ voluntary, harmonious cohabitation.'
 – PoCA 2006: Child marriage voidable on attaining majority. Minor can repudiate. NOT automatically void.
 – Court: Atta satta 'commodifies children, suppresses consent' — girls = 'transferable obligations.'

Key Laws HMA 1955 · PoCA 2006 · DV Act 2005 · Muklawa custom · matrimonial cruelty standard
CLAT Angle Child marriage · matrimonial law · custom vs fundamental rights · standard of proof

     17      CRIMINAL LAW


Bail Under UAPA — Conflicting SC Bench Rulings
K.A. Najeeb (2021) vs NIA v Watali (2019): Which Prevails?

Court: Supreme Court of India | Law: UAPA Sec 43D(5) · Article 21 · NIA Act

 – SC granted bail to Kashmiri man in narco-terror case; exposed dangerous divergence in UAPA bail law.
 – UAPA Sec 43D(5): Bail refused if court believes prima facie case exists — very high threshold.
 – 2019 Watali ruling (2-judge): Courts must accept state's case at face value, no merits examination.
 – 2021 Najeeb ruling (3-judge, CJI NV Ramana): Prolonged incarceration with no trial end = bail under Art 21.
 – Bench (Justices Nagarathna + Ujjal Bhuyan): 'Smaller bench bound by larger bench ratio' — Najeeb wins.
 – Multiple 2-judge benches sidestepped Najeeb: 2024 Gurwinder Singh; Jan 2026 Northeast Delhi riots case.
 – Correct course: Smaller bench disagreeing must refer matter to CJI for larger bench constitution.

Key Laws UAPA Sec 43D(5) · NIA v Zahoor Ahmed Shah Watali (2019) · K.A. Najeeb (2021) · Art 21
CLAT Angle UAPA bail · judicial discipline · stare decisis · Art 21 undertrial rights · bench hierarchy


    18       JUDICIAL REFORMS


Why India's Courts Are Slow — The Court Manager Problem
5 Crore Pending Cases · 13th Finance Commission's Failed Experiment

Court: SC May 2025 Order on Court Managers | Law: 13th Finance Commission Scheme · SC Directives

 – 5 crore+ pending cases; delays cost an estimated 1.5–2% of GDP annually.
 – 13th Finance Commission (2010–15): Recommended MBA-qualified court managers at district & HC level.
 – Rs 300 crore allocated as one-time 5-year grant. Only ~13% utilised.
 – By March 2015: Only ~128 positions filled nationwide. Scheme collapsed after central funding ended.
 – Why it failed: Not institutionalised as permanent cadre; judges resisted parting with admin functions.
 – SC Aug 2018: Issued clear directions on court managers — largely ignored.
 – SC May 2025: All HCs to frame/update service rules within 3 months; states get 3 more months.
 – Core point: Until judges are freed from admin tasks, benefits of digitisation remain limited.

Key Laws 13th Finance Commission scheme · SC directives on court managers · Judicial admin reform
CLAT Angle Judicial reforms · pendency problem · court administration · separation of judicial & admin functions


    19       PROPERTY LAW


MP HC: Bhojshala Was a Temple — ASI Survey Decides
Dhar's Disputed Complex — Religious Character vs Title of Ownership

Court: Madhya Pradesh High Court | Law: Ancient Monuments Act 1904 & 1958 · Evidence Act

 – MP HC May 15: Bhojshala-Kamal Maula complex = temple of Goddess Vagdevi (Saraswati). 242-page judgment.
 – Bench: Justices Vijay Kumar Shukla + Alok Awasthi.
 – Historical finding: Complex linked to Raja Bhoj of Parmar dynasty; Sanskrit learning centre; predates 1034 AD.
 – Muslim claim: 1935 Ailan (princely order) recognised it as mosque. HC: Ailan has no legal constitutional force.
 – Property notified as ancient monument since 1904 — princely state ruler could not override this legally.
 – ASI survey (2024): 7 senior archaeologists; carbon dating used; HC: survey was fair and impartial.
 – Critically: Court did NOT decide title — distinguished from Ayodhya (civil title suit).
 – 2003 arrangement (Hindus puja Tue, Muslims namaz Fri) — portions set aside; ASI continues management.


                                                      CLAT 2027 Preparation · @CLAT_Vision

@CLAT_Vision                                               Law Articles · May 2026                                     Page 9


Key Laws Ancient Monuments Act 1904 & 1958 · Waqf Act · Evidence Act (historical documentary evidence)
CLAT Angle Property disputes · religious places · Places of Worship Act · ASI survey validity · historical evidence


   20        RTI LAW


Why BCCI Is Not a 'Public Authority' Under RTI Act
CIC 2026 Order — Section 2(h) Definition Explained

Court: Central Information Commission (CIC) | Law: RTI Act 2005 Sec 2(h) · Article 12

 – CIC May 18: BCCI is NOT a 'public authority' under RTI Act Sec 2(h).
 – RTI Sec 2(h): Public authority = body established by Constitution/Parliament/state law/govt notification; also
   bodies 'substantially financed' by govt.
 – BCCI: Registered under TN Societies Registration Act 1975 — private association, not a statutory body.
 – CIC: 'Body created by statute' (SBI) ≠ 'body governed by statute after private formation' (BCCI).
 – Control test: Office-bearers elected internally; no govt nominee; decisions don't need govt approval.
 – Financing test: BCCI earns via media rights, sponsorships, tickets. Govt stadiums use ≠ substantial financing.
 – National Sports Governance Act 2025: Bodies receiving govt grants = public authority to that extent. BCCI gets
   none.
 – Zee Telefilms v UoI (SC 2005): BCCI not 'State' under Article 12.
 – But: BCCI can face writ jurisdiction under Article 226 for public function performance.

Key Laws RTI Act 2005 Sec 2(h) · Article 12 · Zee Telefilms (SC 2005) · National Sports Governance Act 2025
CLAT Angle RTI Act · public authority definition · Article 12 · BCCI governance · right to information


     21      NUCLEAR LAW


SHANTI Act's Nuclear Liability Limits Under SC Scrutiny
Articles 14, 19, 21 vs Operator Liability Caps

Court: Supreme Court of India | Law: SHANTI Act · Nuclear Damage Act 2010 · Shriram Oleum 1987

 – SC May 19: Challenge to SHANTI Act described as 'very sensitive legislative policy issue.'
 – SHANTI = Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India Act.
 – 2010 Act: No-fault regime; Rs 1,500 crore cap; Sec 17(b) gave operators recourse against suppliers.
 – SHANTI fragments liability: Rs 100 cr (small reactors) Rs 300 cr (medium) Rs 3,000 cr (large).
 – Supplier accountability: Old Sec 17(b) gone. SHANTI Sec 16: Recourse only if in contract or intentional damage.
 – Shriram Oleum 1987 (Absolute Liability): Hazardous enterprise liable for all damage, independent of fault.
 – Petition: Rs 100 crore cap vs Chernobyl (USD 235–700 bn), Fukushima (USD 440–445 bn) — 'thousand times'
   lower.
 – Sec 67: Claims extinguished after 10 yrs (property) / 20 yrs (personal injury) — radiation effects emerge decades
   later.
 – Sec 81 bars civil courts; Sec 39 classifies nuclear info as restricted, overriding RTI Act.

Key Laws SHANTI Act · Nuclear Damage Act 2010 · Shriram Oleum 1987 (Absolute Liability) · Arts 14, 19, 21
CLAT Angle Nuclear liability · absolute liability doctrine · polluter pays · Art 21 · statutory caps vs constitution


    22       ELECTION LAW


SC SIR Ruling — EC to Report Deleted Names for Citizenship Test
Special Intensive Revision of Electoral Rolls Upheld with Safeguards

Court: Supreme Court of India | Law: Citizenship Act 1955 · RoP Act 1951



                                                      CLAT 2027 Preparation · @CLAT_Vision

@CLAT_Vision                                                Law Articles · May 2026                                        Page 10


 – SC upheld constitutional validity of EC's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
 – EC empowered to examine citizenship questions during roll revision — but power is 'prima facie and contextual.'
 – Deletion from voter list ≠ declaration of non-citizenship — but deleted persons face citizenship adjudication.
 – EC must refer deleted-name cases within 4 weeks to Competent Authority under Citizenship Act 1955.
 – Burden shifts to deleted individual: Must prove citizenship before next elections.
 – Lal Babu Hussein (1995 SC): Electoral roll entry carries presumption of regularity — but it's rebuttable.
 – SC: SIR initially raised concerns; judicial interventions rendered process 'constitutionally compliant.'
 – SC directed publication of ~65 lakh excluded electors' names with reasons for exclusion.

Key Laws Citizenship Act 1955 · RoP Act 1951 · Foreigners Act · Lal Babu Hussein v Electoral Registration Officer (1995)
CLAT Angle Electoral rolls · citizenship determination · SIR process · EC powers · burden of proof


    23       TAX LAW


SC Upholds Retrospective 28% GST on Online Gaming
Rs 2.5 Lakh Crore Tax Demand — Existential Blow to Sector

Court: Supreme Court of India | Law: GST Act · PROG Act 2025 · GST Council Oct 2023 Amendment

 – SC May 27: 28% GST on online gaming applied retrospectively to pre-Oct 2023 revenue.
 – Bench: Justices JB Pardiwala + R Mahadevan. Total demands: ~Rs 2.5 lakh crore.
 – Industry argued: 28% rate should apply only prospectively from Oct 1, 2023 (GST Council amendment date).
 – SC: 2023 amendments are 'clarificatory' retrospective application valid.
 – Taxable value: Full face value of bets/deposits — NOT just platform fee or gross gaming revenue.
 – Real-money gaming = gambling for GST regardless of skill element.
 – PROG Act 2025: Govt already banned online real-money gaming — national security, money laundering
   concerns.
 – Karnataka HC had given relief to Gameskraft (Rs 21,000 crore notice) — SC overturned.
 – Expert: Most companies shut down or pivoted — recovering these demands may be practically impossible.

Key Laws GST Act · PROG Act 2025 · GST Council Resolution Oct 2023 · skill vs chance doctrine
CLAT Angle GST levy · retrospective taxation · online gaming regulation · PROG Act 2025


   24        PUBLIC SAFETY LAW


SC Raps States on Stray Dogs — ABC Rules 2023 Upheld
Article 21 Includes Right to Move Freely Without Fear of Dog Attacks

Court: Supreme Court of India | Law: PCA Act 1960 · ABC Rules 2023 · Article 21 · Art 51A(g)

 – SC May 19: Upheld ABC Rules 2023; states must implement thoroughly. 'State cannot be a passive spectator.'
 – Bench: Justices Vikram Nath + Sandeep Mehta + NV Anjaria. Trigger: 6-yr-old Delhi girl died of dog bite + rabies.
 – Article 21: Right to life includes right to move freely in public spaces without fear of dog attacks.
 – ABC Rules 2023: Sterilisation + anti-rabies vaccination = primary control. Dogs released back to same locality.
 – ABC Rules do NOT permit indiscriminate killing. Euthanasia only for rabid/terminally ill/dangerous dogs.
 – SC: Every district must have at least one fully functional ABC centre.
 – NHAI + States: Coordinated mechanism for stray animals on highways and expressways.
 – Constitutional tension: Article 51A(g) (compassion for living creatures) vs Articles 19 & 21 (citizen safety).
 – Non-compliance may invite contempt proceedings against defaulting authorities.
